short_definition: An emergency fund is money set aside in an easy-to-access, low-risk account to cover unexpected costs such as job loss, medical bills or urgent repairs without borrowing.
explanation: An emergency fund is usually kept in a separate savings account, so you can reach it quickly but won't be tempted to spend it day to day. A common rule of thumb is to cover several months of essential expenses. The right amount depends on how stable your income is, who depends on you, and what insurance you have.

It matters because emergencies are what push many people into high-interest debt. With a cash buffer, a broken car or a gap in income stays an inconvenience instead of becoming a debt spiral. It also means you don't have to sell investments at a bad time.

The trade-off is that cash held for safety usually earns less than long-term investments and can lose buying power to inflation. Choose an account that is easy to access and, where your country offers it, covered by a deposit protection scheme. Check the coverage limits with your bank or regulator.
example: Example (illustrative numbers only): Sam's essential monthly costs (rent, food, utilities, transport, minimum debt payments) are 1,500. A three-month target is 4,500 and a six-month target is 9,000. Sam saves 300 a month automatically and reaches the three-month target in 15 months.
common_mistake: Investing emergency money in shares or crypto for higher returns. Then it may be worth much less exactly when you need it.
title: Emergency Fund
